title: Specificity, Inheritance and the Cascade
summary: Sometimes two CSS rules choose the same part of a page. The browser has rules for deciding which value wins.
introduction: Sometimes two CSS rules choose the same part of a page. The browser has rules for deciding which value wins. Start with two different colours for one heading. Learn how importance, selector strength and order affect the result.
learningObjectives: Calculate the specificity of a selector and predict which rule wins
Explain the steps of the cascade: origin, importance, layers, specificity and order
Use inherit, initial, unset and revert, and avoid !important

blocks.text: When several declarations target the same property on the same element, the browser sorts them by the criteria below and the first criterion that differs decides. Most day-to-day conflicts are settled by the last two, but the earlier ones explain the surprising cases.

items: **Origin and importance.** Styles come from the browser (user agent), the user and the author (you). Normal author declarations beat user and browser defaults. `!important` reverses the order: an important browser or user declaration beats everything of yours.
**Inline styles.** A declaration in a `style` attribute beats any author rule with a selector, except `!important` rules.
**Cascade layers.** For normal declarations, a later `@layer` beats earlier layers, and declarations outside any layer beat all layered ones (with `!important` the layer order is reversed).
**Specificity.** The more specific selector wins (details below).
**Order of appearance.** Everything else equal, the declaration the browser read last wins.

blocks.text: Specificity is a triple **A-B-C**. A counts id selectors, B counts class selectors, attribute selectors and pseudo-classes, and C counts type selectors and pseudo-elements. Compare A first; only if it ties compare B, then C. No amount of classes ever beats one id. The universal selector `*`, combinators and `:where()` add nothing; `:is()`, `:not()` and `:has()` take the specificity of their most specific argument.

blocks.text: Work it through: the first paragraph matches all four rules. `#intro p` has an id, so its A value of 1 beats every other rule regardless of their B and C values. The second paragraph is not inside `#intro`, so the contest is between `p` (0-0-1) and the two `.text` rules (0-1-0 each): the class rules win on B, and between the two of them the later one, orange, wins on order.

Low, flat specificity is what makes a stylesheet easy to change: when most rules are a single class (0-1-0), any later single class can override them. Style with classes rather than ids, avoid long descendant chains, and wrap base styles that components should override in `:where()`, which contributes nothing, so `:where(ul, ol) { padding: 0; }` can be overridden by any class at all. The `!important` flag is the opposite strategy and should be rare.

blocks.title: !important does not fix specificity, it escalates it
blocks.text: Adding `!important` wins today and loses tomorrow, when the next override needs an `!important` with a more specific selector, and the one after that another. The fix for a rule that will not override is to *lower* the specificity of the rule in the way: replace the id with a class, shorten the chain, or move the base style into a cascade layer. Keep `!important` for utility classes that must win by design.

Some properties pass their computed value down to descendants unless a descendant sets its own. Text-related properties inherit: `color`, every `font-*` property, `line-height`, `letter-spacing`, `text-align`, `list-style`, `visibility`, `cursor`. Box-related properties do not: `width`, `height`, `margin`, `padding`, `border`, `background`, `display` and `position` apply only to the element they are set on. Form controls are the common surprise: browsers give `button`, `input` and `select` their own font, so a page's typography stops at them until you tell them to inherit.

rows: Take the parent's computed value, even for properties that do not inherit by default
Reset to the property's specification default (`color: initial` is black, not the parent's colour)
`inherit` for inherited properties, `initial` for the others
Undo author styles and fall back to the browser's or user's styles

blocks.text: `@layer` groups rules into named layers whose order you declare up front. Between layers, order beats specificity: a one-class rule in a later layer overrides an id-based rule in an earlier layer. Rules outside any layer beat every layer. The usual arrangement is reset, then base, then components, with third-party CSS imported into a low layer so that your own rules always win without specificity games. All current browsers support layers.

blocks.title: Read the cascade in developer tools
blocks.text: Select an element and look at the *Styles* panel: rules are listed from the one that wins downwards, and every declaration that lost is struck through. Hovering a selector shows its specificity in current browsers. When a style will not apply, this view tells you *which* rule beat it, and why.

questions.question: Which selector has the highest specificity?
questions.explanation: `#main` is 1-0-0. Ids are compared first, so a single id beats three classes (0-3-0) and four types (0-0-4). `:where()` always has 0-0-0.

questions.question: `:where(.card)` has the same specificity as `.card`.
questions.explanation: `:where()` contributes zero specificity whatever it contains, which is exactly why it is used for base styles that should be easy to override.
